topics.title: Submarine Relief and Ocean Floor Features

concepts.label: Ocean Relief: The Landscape of the Ocean Floor
concepts.cardText: Oceans cover most of our planet and conceal many secrets. Just as land has mountains, valleys and plains, the ocean floor has landforms together known as submarine relief or ocean relief, including underwater mountains, valleys, plateaus and trenches. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth, while the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range, hidden beneath the ocean. Some underwater mountains like Mauna Kea (Hawai'i) are even taller than Mount Everest. Important features include seamounts, often volcanic, some of which are flattened by wave action over millennia into guyots; ocean trenches, the deepest parts of the ocean; the Mid-Ocean Ridge, an immense underwater range formed by volcanic activity; the abyssal plain, the vast, flat, deep ocean floor; the continental shelf, the shallow submerged edge of a continent rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas; and the steep continental slope marking the true edge of a continent.

topics.title: Movements of Ocean Water: Waves, Tides and Currents

concepts.label: Waves and the Coast They Shape
concepts.cardText: The water in the oceans is constantly in motion. Waves, tides and currents help shape the Earth's surface, support marine life, aid fishing and travel, and even influence climate. When the surface of the ocean rises and falls alternately, it is called a wave. Waves are primarily caused by winds blowing across the water, and they carry energy across the oceans over long distances, with crests (high peaks) and troughs (lower valleys). Waves are often called coastal architects as they shape the shoreline through erosion and sediment transport, creating erosional features such as sea caves, arches, sea stacks and stumps, and depositional features such as beaches. During storms, strong winds can generate huge waves that damage coastlines. The giant waves majorly caused by underwater earthquakes are called tsunamis, extremely destructive, which on reaching the shore may attain a run-up height of up to 30 metres or even more.

concepts.label: Tides: Spring and Neap Tides and Their Uses
concepts.cardText: Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water that occur twice a day in most parts of the world: high tide (flood tide) when water rises to its highest level and covers much of the shore, and low tide (ebb tide) when it falls to its lowest level. Spring tides occur when the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are aligned in a straight line, on full moon and new moon days: the combined gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon causes unusually high high tides and unusually low low tides. Neap tides occur when the Moon is in its first and third quarter, when the Sun's and Moon's pulls act in different directions, so the difference between high and low tide becomes smaller. Tides matter for navigation, as high tide raises the water level and lets ships enter harbours, with the Gulf of Khambhat having a tidal range of about 12 metres; high tides support fishing as fish move close to shore; and tidal energy can generate electricity, with the Gulf of Kutch, the Gulf of Khambhat and the Sundarbans identified as suitable sites in India.

concepts.label: Ocean Currents: Warm and Cold Streams and Their Effects
concepts.cardText: Ocean currents are continuous streams of water that flow across the ocean surface in definite directions. They are caused by winds, the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force), differences in temperature and salinity, and the shape of continents and ocean basins. The Coriolis force deflects any free moving object to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Currents flowing from warmer regions are warm currents and those from colder regions are cold currents, shown on maps in red and blue. The Gulf Stream, a warm current from the Gulf of Mexico, flows towards Norway and keeps its waters relatively warm, so sea ice does not form easily there despite its high latitude. The Labrador Current, a cold current along the east coast of Canada, carries freezing water and supports sea ice and icebergs even at lower latitudes. Where warm and cold currents meet are fishing grounds, rich in nutrients and supporting a large variety of fish.

topics.title: Ocean Hazards and Early Warning Systems

concepts.label: Cyclones, Tsunamis and Early Warning Systems
concepts.cardText: Oceans and seas can give rise to sudden hazards such as cyclones, large rotating storms, and tsunamis, giant waves caused by earthquakes. To protect people, scientists have developed Early Warning Systems that work like giant alarm systems for coastal areas: they help detect cyclones and tsunamis, predict disasters and issue timely warnings so that people can evacuate and stay safe. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (26 December 2004) claimed around 2,30,000 lives, and the scale of the disaster led many countries to set up tsunami early warning systems. India set up the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) with a real-time network of tsunami detection buoys. The tsunami warning system works through detection by seismic stations, tracking by tide gauges and radars, confirmation by ocean bottom pressure recorders, and warning dissemination via satellite, SMS and other channels. For cyclones, India uses cyclone warning services, the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) for shelters, and INCOIS and IMD's Storm Surge Early Warning System; the GEMINI device sends alerts to fishermen. Public awareness and training are equally important.

keyPoints.text: The tsunami early warning system works in stages. A network of seismic stations detects undersea earthquakes in real time. Coastal tide gauges and radars monitor changes in sea level to track the arrival and movement of tsunami waves. Ocean Bottom Pressure Recorders placed on the seafloor detect the passage of tsunami waves, confirming the threat. Alerts are transmitted via satellite to government agencies and sent directly to officials and the public through SMS and other communication channels. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre sends alerts to the Government of India, which informs state governments and emergency response teams.

checks.criterion: Describes the tsunami warning chain: seismic stations detect undersea earthquakes, tide gauges and radars track the waves, bottom pressure recorders confirm the threat, and alerts go by satellite, SMS and other channels from the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre to governments and the public.

keyPoints.text: India has several Cyclone Warning Services and Marine Weather Services that monitor storms along both the eastern and western coasts. The Government of India has launched the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project to build cyclone shelters, strengthen warning systems, and improve emergency response mechanisms. INCOIS, in collaboration with the IMD, has established the Storm Surge Early Warning System. The GEMINI device is a handheld device for fishermen that receives satellite information and transmits it to mobile phones, with alerts in local languages about high waves, strong winds, cyclone and tsunami warnings.

topics.title: Marine Resources and the Blue Economy

concepts.label: Marine Resources and Their Significance
concepts.cardText: Oceans are vast storehouses of resources. The materials and features found in oceans that have intrinsic or economic value are called marine resources, broadly classified into marine living resources and marine non-living resources. They include fish and seafood, biodiversity, oil and natural gas, minerals, sand and gravel, renewable blue energy such as tidal and wave energy, tourism potential and ecosystems such as coral reefs. Marine resources are vital for food security, economic activities and a healthy environment. Fish are a major source of protein and fishing and aquaculture support livelihoods; offshore oil and gas and 'blue energy' from tides and waves provide energy; about 90% of global trade by volume is carried by sea and coastal tourism is a multi-billion dollar industry; sand, gravel and deep-sea minerals are materials; and the sacred conch and cowrie shells, once used as currency, show cultural significance. Marine resources must be used responsibly without disturbing marine ecosystems.

concepts.label: The Blue Economy and Sustainable Use of the Ocean
concepts.cardText: The World Bank defines the Blue Economy as 'the sustainable use of ocean resources to promote economic growth, improved livelihoods, and jobs, while preserving the health of the marine ecosystem'. It balances three aims: economic growth, improved livelihoods and jobs, and ecosystem health. This concept is enshrined in the UN's Sustainable Development Goal 14: Life Below Water, whose key aims include reducing marine pollution, protecting and conserving marine ecosystems and areas, addressing ocean acidification, regulating fishing, eliminating harmful subsidies and increasing economic benefits. Blue Economy is the future: sustainable growth powered by healthy oceans.

topics.title: Maritime Zones and Rules of the Sea

concepts.label: Maritime Zones: Territorial Waters, Contiguous Zone, EEZ and High Seas
concepts.cardText: Maritime zones are different areas of the ocean defined by international law. The sea area closest to a country is its territorial waters, over which the country has near-complete control, subject to the right of innocent passage for foreign ships; the government can make laws relating to customs, immigration and pollution control there. Beyond lies the contiguous zone, extending from the baseline up to 24 nautical miles, where the country has limited control over customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration. Beyond it are the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs), extending up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, defined under UNCLOS, where a country has special rights to use ocean resources such as fish, oil and gas, though other ships may pass peacefully and the country does not fully own the waters. Beyond all EEZs lie the high seas, international waters covering about 64 per cent of the world's oceans, part of the global commons, where all countries enjoy equal rights of navigation, fishing, overflight and laying cables; on the high seas the laws of the flag state apply.

keyPoints.text: The sea area closest to a country is called its territorial waters, over which the country has near-complete control, subject to the right of innocent passage for foreign ships. The government can make laws relating to customs, immigration, and pollution control in this zone. Beyond this lies the contiguous zone, extending from the baseline up to 24 nautical miles, where the country has limited control over customs, fiscal matters, and illegal immigration. Innocent Passage allows foreign ships to pass through the territorial waters as long as they do not threaten its peace, good order, or security.

checks.criterion: Describes the inner zones: territorial waters (near-complete control, subject to innocent passage by foreign ships that do not threaten peace, order or security) and the contiguous zone up to 24 nautical miles with limited control over customs, fiscal matters and illegal immigration.

keyPoints.text: Beyond the contiguous zone, lie the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs), which extend from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, and are defined under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). In these zones, a country has special rights to use ocean resources, such as fish, oil, and gas, although ships from other countries may still pass through peacefully, and the country does not fully own or control the waters of the EEZ. Beyond the EEZs lie the high seas, also known as international waters, covering about 64 per cent of the world's oceans, which do not belong to any single country and are part of the global commons. On the high seas, the laws of the flag state apply.

concepts.label: International Maritime Rules and Why They Matter
concepts.cardText: To ensure that activities at sea remain safe, fair and peaceful, countries follow international rules and agreements known as maritime law. These laws regulate how ships operate and move; protect the marine environment; address piracy, terrorism, natural disasters and accidents; safeguard trade routes; and help settle disputes between countries. Just as there are traffic rules on land, ships follow the 'rules of the road at sea', COLREGs (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea), including a proper lookout, which side to pass, give-way and stand-on vessels, safe speed and the use of lights and sound signals. The MARPOL Convention aims at reducing pollution from ships. These rules help keep the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of resources, enabling cooperation without conflict while protecting marine life, ships, sailors and coastal communities; without them the oceans could become dangerous and chaotic. UNCLOS helps define maritime zones and settle disputes.

keyPoints.text: To ensure that activities at sea remain safe, fair, and peaceful, countries follow a set of international rules and agreements known as maritime law or maritime regulations. These laws regulate how ships operate and move; protect the marine environment; address issues such as piracy, terrorism, natural disasters, and accidents; safeguard trade routes; and help settle disputes between countries. Just as there are traffic rules on land, ships must follow rules of the road at sea, known as COLREGs, to avoid accidents, and the MARPOL Convention is an important international agreement aimed at reducing pollution from ships.
keyPoints.followUp: What are the 'traffic rules' for ships, and which agreement tries to stop ships polluting the sea?

checks.criterion: States that international maritime law keeps the sea safe, fair and peaceful by regulating ships, protecting the marine environment, safeguarding trade routes and settling disputes, with COLREGs as the rules of the road at sea and MARPOL reducing pollution from ships.

keyPoints.text: International maritime rules, regulations, and agreements help keep the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of ocean resources. These rules enable countries to cooperate in using marine resources without conflict while protecting marine life, ships, sailors, and coastal communities. Without such regulations, the oceans could become dangerous and chaotic, with increased pollution, accidents, collisions, and disputes over resources. International laws such as UNCLOS help define maritime zones and settle disputes among countries.

checks.criterion: States that maritime rules keep the oceans safe and ensure fair, sustainable use, let countries cooperate without conflict, protect marine life and people, and that without them the oceans could become dangerous and chaotic; UNCLOS defines maritime zones and settles disputes.
